title: SLO Steering Autoscaler & Latency Hedging — PRD (raw)
content:
Context and problem statement:

We operate Dedicated pools where tenants bring committed reservations and occasionally need to burst. Current autoscalers are primarily resource-driven (GPU utilization, node counts) and schedule prewarm/decommit purely on capacity forecasts. This leaves a gap: tenant-facing SLOs (p99 latency targets and error budgets) are not tightly coupled to autoscaler decisions, which causes either over-provisioning to guarantee SLOs or SLO violations during microbursts. We need an autoscaling layer that explicitly "steers" toward tenant SLOs and uses soft hedges to reduce the tail risk of latency spikes while preserving cost efficiency.

Goal (what success looks like):
- Reduce p99 latency SLO violations during demand spikes by >= 60% for tenants using burst features (measured across a 3-month window).
- Keep Dedicated pool cost overhead for hedging below +10% relative to existing autoscaler baseline across steady workloads.
- Provide transparent controls for tenants (priority class, max-burst-credit spend rate, latency SLAs vs cost).
- Offer operators an actionable simulator and runbook for capacity emergency scenarios.

Non-goals:
- Replace node-level autoscalers (k8s/gpu autoscaling) — this sits above those systems.
- Full market-based bursting (tokenized auctions) — out of scope for initial MLP.

Design overview (high-level):
- SLO steering layer: a controller that consumes tenant-level SLOs (p50/p90/p99 latency targets, error budget window) and runtime signals (queue length, in-flight tokens, KV cache hit rates, tail-latency deviation) and computes a probabilistic hedging requirement (hedge size) per tenant for a short horizon (30s-5m).
- Hedging mechanisms (soft hedges): three orthogonal techniques used singly or in combination:
  1) Fast prewarm pool (ephemeral warm workers): a small pool of already-initialized workers kept ready by predictive short-term stakes.
  2) Micro-burst credit buffer: per-tenant soft credits that allow short duration higher concurrency; credits decay and are regenerated on low utilization.
  3) Priority spill lanes: lightweight priority classification that routes excess requests to lower-cost model variants or degraded policy when hedges are exhausted.
- Autoscaler integration: SLO steering outputs a hedging vector that the underlying autoscaler consumes along with utilization forecasts. Autoscaler must honor latency-hedge delta as a soft constraint (prefer to add capacity but can fallback to priority spill lanes).
- Feedback & learning: continuous telemetry of actual latency outcomes vs predicted hedge helps tune the steering model and hedge sizing parameters.

Key flows and decision points:
1) Tenant declares SLO profile when reserving capacity: {p99_target_ms, burst_priority (low/normal/high), max_credit_rate}. This is surfaced in the Console and API.
2) Real-time signals ingested by the steering layer: CPU/GPU util %, queue depth, recent token generation rate, per-model kv-cache hit ratio, model size, recent tail-latency deltas.
3) Steering computes hedge demand per tenant for next horizon; summary: {required_ephemeral, required_credit_delta, recommended_spill_action}.
4) Autoscaler attempts to provision ephemeral instances within budget; if unsuccessful, it triggers priority spill lanes and reduces credit allotment to avoid cross-tenant impact.
5) Observability: per-tenant dashboard shows hedge consumption, spend, p99 trend, and the reason for any spill.

Operational controls and UI: 
- Console: SLO tab on Dedicated tenancy page where tenant admins can set p99 targets and peek at historical trade-offs.
- Operator toggles: global hedge budget, per-pool max-ephemerals, cost-floor override, emergency preemption policy.
- API: POST /tenants/{id}/slo to set SLO and credit params. GET /tenants/{id}/hedge-report returns last-5m hedging decisions for debugging.

Metrics & success instrumentation:
- Primary: p99 latency violations per-tenant per-hour, hedging-induced cost overhead (estimated $/hour), percent of bursts served from ephemeral vs spills.
- Secondary: prediction error (hedge_capacity_requested / capacity_needed), credit-drawdown events, cross-tenant interference alerts.

Simulation plan (must be run before MLP):
- Build a 'spiky-tenant' simulator (Python) that replays real traffic traces (samples from last 6 months) and injects synthetic microbursts with tunable amplitude and shape.
- Evaluate several steering heuristics: fixed headroom percent, risk-aware probabilistic (95% CI hedge), adaptive buffer tied to in-flight cache hit rate.
- Run A/B sims: existing autoscaler vs SLO-steering autoscaler across 1000 synthetic tenants and measure p99 and cost delta.
- Deliverable: simulation report with recommended default heuristic and parameter ranges.

Security and multi-tenant isolation considerations: 
- Hedging must not allow one tenant to starve another. All ephemeral capacity is tagged and accounting enforced at the infra layer. Credit overspend is enforced via the API gate and token-level throttling.
- Priority spill lanes will execute on well-defined degraded model variants that are trained to avoid data leakage (no cross-tenant cache reuse).

Failure modes and runbook (high level):
- Symptom: sudden cluster-wide p99 spike.
  - Triage: check steering decisions vs time-series; did steering request hedges and were they denied?
  - If steering requested but autoscaler failed: roll emergency prewarm (operator toggle) to immediate ephemeral allocation and enact temporary cost-floor.
  - If steering did not request: examine telemetry feed (queue depth / cache hit) and check for telemetry ingestion lag.
- Symptom: one tenant consumes >80% of ephemeral pool.
  - Triage: enforce per-tenant ephemeral quota and throttle credit spend. Notify tenant SRE and apply spill policy.

Open questions / engineering risks:
- How to compute hedge sizing reliably across different model families (small LMs vs large 70B)? Cache behavior differs greatly. Propose per-model uplift factors in the steering model.
- Latency vs cost tradeoff: what is acceptable percent overhead by default? Need product discussion (marketing & sales impact).
- Integration complexity: autoscaler (k8s cluster-autoscaler / custom broker) must be extended to accept time-scoped hedges; evaluate compatibility.
- Billing: how to surface ephemeral/hege usage on invoices and tie to reserved commitments?

Immediate next steps (2-week sprint):
- Sprint priority A: implement simulator + baseline runs with 3 heuristics (Diego).
- Sprint priority B: API + Console SLO toggles mockups (Priya & Hannah).
- Sprint priority C: integration spike with autoscaler shim (Ben) to prototype soft-constraint signaling.
- Sprint priority D: draft runbook and operator emergency toggle spec (Aisha).

Notes to self:
- Keep default hedges conservative for initial rollout (e.g., 20% ephemeral cap, credit regen 1 credit / 30s).
- Add a "quiet period" so hedges don't oscillate on short bursts less than 10s.
- Coordinate with infra release for tagging ephemeral instances to make billing visible within console.

References and context links:
- See linked artifacts above for Linear ticket and runtime PR. Also check internal slides: /shared_drives/product/dedicated/latency-hedging-slides-2025-09.txt (older sketch)

Appendix: example tenant SLO profile (UI representation):
- Name: "search-proxy-annotations"
- p50: 40ms, p90: 120ms, p99: 350ms (target)
- burst_priority: high
- max_credit_rate: 10 credits / minute
- preferred_spill_action: degrade-to-lite-model

End of draft.

-- aisha
